{{Short description|Order-continuous function on ordinals}}
{{one source |date=March 2024}}
{{about|order-continuous functions on ordinals |the common concept|continuous function}}

In [[set theory]], a '''continuous function''' is a [[sequence]] of [[ordinal number|ordinal]]s such that the values assumed at [[limit ordinal|limit stage]]s are the limits ([[Limit superior and limit inferior|limit suprema and limit infima]]) of all values at previous stages. More formally, let ''γ'' be an ordinal, and <math>s := \langle s_{\alpha}| \alpha < \gamma\rangle</math> be a ''γ''-sequence of ordinals.  Then ''s'' is continuous if at every limit ordinal ''β'' < ''γ'',
:<math>s_{\beta} = \limsup\{s_{\alpha}: \alpha < \beta\} = \inf \{ \sup\{s_{\alpha}: \delta \leq \alpha < \beta\} : \delta < \beta\} </math>

and
:<math>s_{\beta} = \liminf\{s_{\alpha}: \alpha < \beta\} = \sup \{ \inf\{s_{\alpha}: \delta \leq \alpha < \beta\} : \delta < \beta\} \,.</math>

Alternatively, if ''s'' is an [[increasing function]] then ''s'' is continuous if ''s'': ''γ'' → range(''s'') is a [[continuous (topology)|continuous function]] when the sets are each equipped with the [[order topology]]. These continuous functions are often used in [[cofinality|cofinalities]] and [[cardinal numbers]].

A [[normal function]] is a function that is both continuous and [[monotonic function|strictly increasing]].
